title: Tarbut and the Making of Hebrew Education in Sokółka
summary: The school and its pupils reveal how Sokółka’s Jewish families invested in modern Hebrew education and a shared cultural future.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Eighth-grade Tarbut School class in Sokolka

editorialContent:
## A school—and a language for the future

In Sokółka, Tarbut meant more than a place to take lessons. It brought Hebrew into the daily life of children growing up in a town where Jewish education also included traditional religious schools, Polish state schooling and, for some, a Polish gymnasium. The memorial book recalls a school that taught in Hebrew and connected learning with Zionist hopes. The wider history places it within a transregional movement: Tarbut schools linked local classrooms to a modern Hebrew educational network and to the ideal of Jewish national renewal.

The memorial book preserves two different starting points that should not be made into one exact foundation date. One account says a Hebrew school was founded in 1904, though the printed date is unclear in the surviving transcription. Another describes a Sokółka branch of the “Culture” school opening after the war between Poland and Russia, affiliated with a central organization in Warsaw. The book’s English translation calls that conflict the Polish-Russian war; it does not give a precise opening year for the local branch. The evidence therefore suggests an earlier Hebrew-school tradition followed by the later Tarbut institution, but does not establish exactly how one became the other.

In the memorial book’s account of local education, several schools taught Hebrew or combined religious learning with general subjects. It names Hillel Levine, Nathaniel Kaplan, Nahum Kunsht and Haim Yerushavski among the teachers associated with Hebrew schooling. A separate remembrance identifies [Nathaniel Kaplan](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_05f01ce22bb03bcaae0832f1) as Tarbut’s founder and manager, describing his persistence in keeping the school open despite official disfavor and uncertain support. These are memories written by former residents, not a surviving administrative file; they convey how the school’s place in town was remembered.

## What a Tarbut education offered

According to the memorial book, the Sokółka Tarbut branch was affiliated with the [Warsaw Tarbut center](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_afe5b2a7a9924ae70e25257b). Lessons were conducted in Hebrew. Alongside Bible study, pupils learned grammar, arithmetic, geography and history; the account also mentions gymnastics and singing. This combination made Hebrew both a language of study and a language for modern subjects and shared activity.

The wider history helps explain the school’s connection to Warsaw. The Tarbut movement developed as a network of Hebrew-language schools in interwar Poland and elsewhere in Eastern Europe. Its institutions included elementary and secondary schools, teacher-training, libraries and educational publishing. The network was associated with Zionist groups, while its curriculum could combine Hebrew and Jewish history with secular subjects. Sokółka’s school thus belonged to a broader project: making Hebrew a living language of education, not only of prayer or textual study. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbut))

But the book’s account also places Tarbut beside other choices, not above them. It describes traditional heders and the Talmud Torah, and notes that a Polish government school with eight classes and a Polish gymnasium also educated Jewish children. The earlier schools it calls *heder m’tukan* combined religious study with mathematics, history and geography, with lessons in Hebrew. The town’s educational landscape was therefore plural. Tarbut’s distinctiveness lay not simply in teaching Hebrew, but in organizing a modern school around it and associating that education with Zionist ideals.

## The 1927 class: names in a remembered photograph

A photograph caption is one of the memorial book’s most tangible records of student life. One account identifies an eighth-grade class of the Sokółka Tarbut school in 1927, with its teacher, whose surname appears in the English translation as Sudkowitz. From right to left, it names [Yehuda Levin](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_8ed77afc94c344a703ff085f), [Shimon Krugalk](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_11cf8e16216bcc3be7691bc2), [Aba Antakal](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_37f649f59c19847a9bbfeb17), [David Yatom](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_0bfd46902e7ff54a6f829d94), the teacher, [Yaakov Shabransky](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_2848478782201ec04b6d9d22), [Yosef Kapliushnik](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_24298f937a64beee8c0940c6), [Nissan Cohen](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_96ac71c5b5c56316ff64a112), [Yehezkel Piker](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_f48bd1cdfe5f1fc1df5174ef) and [Eliyahu Chinsky](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_0d9d486ae60048ed06e0385d). The supplied records render some names differently—such as Krugalk/Kruglach and Yatom/Tatom—so these forms should not be silently treated as certain standardized spellings.

There is also a discrepancy about the grade. The community photograph caption calls the pupils eighth-graders, while another memorial-book caption identifies a Tarbut class of 1927 as the seventh grade. These may be distinct photographs, or reflect inconsistent captions; the available text does not settle the matter. What can be said is that the book associates a named group of students and a teacher with Tarbut schooling in 1927. It does not provide biographies or later fates for those pupils, and names alone are not enough to identify them in other records.

## Celebrations, play and the town around the school

The book remembers Tarbut not only through classroom subjects but through the rhythms of childhood. In one account, children marched through Sokółka on Lag Ba’Omer, singing a Zionist song before going to the forest for games and a day outdoors. Another Tarbut recollection describes the school’s compact building near the town’s synagogue square, the Schulhof, and the children’s friendships and rivalries. Together, these memories show a school embedded in town life: its pupils moved between lessons, streets, public celebrations and nearby recreation.

Summer bathing and winter games appear in the book’s account of the town’s children. It names the Kuryły River and several bathing places, including [Vodoktsky pools](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_6f0e8765bdac7a07909c707b), [Zavrod under the river](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_e476f45978d232c1240ebbcc) and [Kopalnies](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_53bb9d989d566cc8c221074a). The translation’s spellings are uncertain, and the memorial account does not say that every outing was organized by the school. It does, however, preserve the landscape in which local childhood unfolded.

These recollections matter because they keep Tarbut from becoming only an institutional label. The class photograph gives names; the celebrations and games give a sense of how education might have been lived—through shared language, songs, movement and companionship. Kaplan’s remembrance adds another dimension: he is credited with arranging summer camps and clinics for poorer children and helping create care for orphans. The memorial book presents educational work as inseparable from social responsibility, though its tribute is a community memory rather than an independent assessment.

## A local school in a wider, fragile network

Tarbut’s reach beyond Sokółka is visible in the Warsaw affiliation, but local survival depended on local commitment. The memorial book says the school struggled financially and faced unfriendly authorities; it also describes fundraising through public donors and children’s activities. Such recollections fit the broader history of a movement whose schools spread widely but faced chronic underfunding. The network’s scale cannot tell us how many Sokółka children enrolled in any particular year, and no independent source consulted here confirms the local school’s enrollment figures or the identities and later lives of the 1927 pupils. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbut))

Yad Vashem’s Sokółka ghetto encyclopedia independently confirms that a Tarbut-network school operated in the town before the war, alongside a yeshiva and Zionist, Bundist and Agudath Israel activity. It also records the destruction of Jewish institutions under Soviet rule after 1939. That entry does not discuss Tarbut’s lessons or the 1927 class, so it corroborates the institution’s presence and later context, not the memorial book’s classroom memories. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691))

The school’s meaning in Sokółka therefore rests on both kinds of evidence. The memorial book remembers Hebrew lessons, teachers, a class, outings and a school that tried to include children with fewer resources. The wider record shows how this local effort belonged to an ambitious network of modern Hebrew education—and how vulnerable Jewish institutions became as political rule shifted and then turned violently against the community. Tarbut offered Sokółka’s children a language for learning and a vision of belonging that reached beyond the town, while remaining rooted in its streets and shared life.
